title: CPU Scheduling: FCFS, SJF, Round Robin and Priority
oneLiner: How the OS decides which ready process (running program) gets the CPU next, and how that choice changes waiting time, response time and fairness.
keyTakeaway: Every scheduling algorithm trades one metric for another. First-come first-served is simple and fair in order, but one long job makes everyone behind it wait (the convoy effect). Shortest job first gives the lowest average waiting time, but it needs to know burst lengths in advance and can starve long jobs. Round robin bounds how long anyone waits for a turn, at the cost of more context switches. Priority scheduling serves what matters first and starves what doesn't, unless the scheduler ages waiting processes upward.
explanation:
A CPU core (one independent processing unit; most CPUs have several) runs one thread at a time, so whenever more threads are ready than there are cores, the OS scheduler has to pick. A process is a running program, and a thread is one sequence of instructions inside it; Concurrency & Memory covers both in depth. The textbooks call the unit of work a process with a CPU burst: how long it needs the CPU before it finishes or blocks on I/O (input/output: waiting for the disk, the network or a keyboard). (The lesson Threads vs Processes and the Scheduler, in Concurrency and Memory, covers what a context switch saves and restores. This lesson is about the policy: who goes next.)

Three numbers measure a schedule. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround minus burst: the time spent ready but not running. Response time is the time from arrival until the process first gets the CPU, which is what an interactive user feels. A scheduler is non-preemptive if a process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks, and preemptive if the OS can take the CPU away, normally when the timer interrupt fires (a hardware signal, every few milliseconds, that makes the CPU pause and run the OS) or a more important process becomes ready.

First-come first-served (FCFS) runs processes in arrival order, non-preemptively. It's a plain FIFO (first in, first out) queue, but if a 20 ms job arrives just before three 2 ms jobs, all three wait behind it: the convoy effect. Shortest job first (SJF) picks the ready process with the smallest burst, and is provably optimal for average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules. Its preemptive form, shortest remaining time first (SRTF), switches as soon as a shorter job arrives. The catch for both is that the OS can't know burst lengths in advance; real schedulers estimate them from past behaviour, typically with an exponential average.

Round robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time quantum and then moves it to the back of the queue. With n ready processes and quantum q, nobody waits more than (n minus 1) times q for a turn, which is why RR suits time-sharing systems. A quantum that's too large turns RR back into FCFS; one that's too small spends the CPU on context switches (saving one process's state and loading another's). Priority scheduling runs the most important ready process first (in this lesson a lower number means higher priority, as in Unix nice values). If high-priority work keeps arriving, a low-priority process may never run: starvation. The standard fix is aging, which raises a process's priority the longer it waits.

Real kernels (the kernel is the core of the OS) combine these ideas. A multilevel feedback queue keeps several priority levels with round robin inside each, and demotes processes that use their whole quantum (CPU-bound) while keeping ones that block early (interactive) near the top. Windows uses 32 priority levels with temporary boosts for threads that wake from I/O or own the foreground window. Linux used the Completely Fair Scheduler, which tracks how much CPU time each task has had and runs the one that has had least, and since kernel 6.6 it uses EEVDF, which also accounts for deadlines so latency-sensitive tasks get on the CPU sooner.

In an interview, say which metric you are optimizing before naming an algorithm: throughput, average waiting time, response time for interactive users, or fairness. Then mention the trade-off you're accepting.
